claim: Economist R. A. Radford, a prisoner of war in World War II, described his camp's economy in a 1945 paper.
appears_in: L1 card.how_money_works.001.c1; L57 card.how_money_works.057.c1; L61 card.how_money_works.061.c1
fact_check_evidence: Finance Watch and other accounts: Radford studied economics at Cambridge, was captured in 1942, and published 'The Economic Organisation of a P.O.W. Camp' in Economica in November 1945. (https://www.finance-watch.org/blog/the-perfect-draw-when-cigarettes-became-a-war-camp-currency/ https://syncopate.us/articles/2006/n24a)

claim: In Radford's camp, cigarettes became the normal currency: everyone, including non-smokers, would sell for cigarettes and use them to buy later.
appears_in: L1 card.how_money_works.001.c1; L1 card.how_money_works.001.c2; L6 card.how_money_works.006.c3
fact_check_evidence: The paper's text (reproduced on syncopate.us): 'everyone, including non-smokers, was willing to sell for cigarettes, using them to buy at another time and place. Cigarettes became the normal currency'. Finance Watch: cigarettes rose to the status of currency. (https://syncopate.us/articles/2006/n24a https://www.finance-watch.org/blog/the-perfect-draw-when-cigarettes-became-a-war-camp-currency/)

claim: Trade in Radford's camp started as direct barter before cigarettes took over as currency.
fact_check_evidence: Radford's text: 'Starting with simple direct barter ... more complex exchanges soon became an accepted custom', before cigarettes became the currency. (https://syncopate.us/articles/2006/n24a)

claim: Camp prices were quoted in cigarettes: prisoners called out offers like 'cheese for seven', and laundry cost two cigarettes a garment.
fact_check_evidence: Radford's text: relative values were 'expressed ... in terms of cigarettes'; offers such as 'cheese for seven' (cigarettes); 'Laundrymen advertised at two cigarettes a garment.' (https://syncopate.us/articles/2006/n24a https://courses.cit.cornell.edu/econ4260/out/radford_pow.pdf)

claim: Prisoners held reserves of cigarettes, but cigarettes were also smoked, so when deliveries stopped, stocks ran out and prices fell.
appears_in: L1 card.how_money_works.001.c4; L3 card.how_money_works.003.c3; L31 card.how_money_works.031.c4; L64 card.how_money_works.064.c1
fact_check_evidence: Radford's text: 'many people held reserves'; cigarettes had strong non-monetary demand, and 'when the issue was interrupted, stocks soon ran out, prices fell'. Finance Watch notes cigarettes served as a store of value. (https://syncopate.us/articles/2006/n24a https://www.finance-watch.org/blog/the-perfect-draw-when-cigarettes-became-a-war-camp-currency/)

fact_check_evidence: OpenStax: barter is 'literally trading one good or service for another'. IMF F&D: without money we would be reduced to a barter economy of direct swaps. (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2012/09/basics.htm)

fact_check_evidence: OpenStax defines the double coincidence of wants as each of two people wanting something the other can provide; Britannica's money article says money frees trade from barter's double coincidence. claim: Without money, a car mechanic who wanted food would have to find a farmer with a broken car.
tested_by: L2 question.how_money_works.002.q1; L35 question.how_money_works.035.q3; L41 question.how_money_works.041.q3; L100 question.how_money_works.100.q2
fact_check_evidence: IMF F&D: 'a person who specialized in fixing cars and needed to trade for food would have to find a farmer with a broken car.' OpenStax gives a parallel example of an accountant who must find someone with shoes who wants accounting. (https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/27-1-defining-money-by-its-functions)

claim: Barter with no established measures has no underlying index of value: each exchange stands virtually on its own.
fact_check_evidence: Humphrey's paper (full text copy): barter 'with no established measures of weight and volume means that there can be no underlying index of value / numeraire. Each transaction exists virtually on its own.' OpenStax contrasts this with money as the common ruler. (https://voidnetwork.gr/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/Barter-and-economic-disintegration-by-Caroline-Humphrey.pdf https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/27-1-defining-money-by-its-functions)

claim: Barter makes it hard to buy things later with perishable goods, like a farmer hoping to pay for a tractor in six months with fresh strawberries.
fact_check_evidence: OpenStax: 'if the goods are perishable it may be difficult to exchange them for other goods in the future. Imagine a farmer wanting to buy a tractor in six months using a fresh crop of strawberries.' The St. Louis Fed contrasts money with corn that might rot. (https://www.stlouisfed.org/open-vault/2021/december/what-is-money)

claim: Economists since Adam Smith have told a story in which barter came first and money replaced it once people saw it was more efficient.
fact_check_evidence: Humphrey: orthodox economics, 'which stems at least from Adam Smith', places barter at the most primitive stage, superseded by money. The IMF's basics article also frames money as the escape from barter. (https://voidnetwork.gr/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/Barter-and-economic-disintegration-by-Caroline-Humphrey.pdf https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2012/09/basics.htm)

claim: In 1985, anthropologist Caroline Humphrey concluded that no pure barter economy has ever been described.
fact_check_evidence: Humphrey (Man, 1985): 'No example of a barter economy, pure and simple, has ever been described, let alone the emergence from it of money.' Semantic Scholar lists the paper (Man 20, 48-72). (https://voidnetwork.gr/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/Barter-and-economic-disintegration-by-Caroline-Humphrey.pdf https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Barter-and-Economic-Disintegration-Humphrey/d3ad38ad3326bafa731013e23283cd9f8c9858cb)

claim: Barter tends to take place between people who know one another.
fact_check_evidence: Humphrey's abstract: 'Barter tends to take place between people who know one another'. (https://voidnetwork.gr/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/Barter-and-economic-disintegration-by-Caroline-Humphrey.pdf)

claim: Salt made good money partly because it is a commodity that nearly everyone needs.

claim: Elizabeth Warren and her daughter Amelia Warren Tyagi popularized the 50/30/20 rule in their book All Your Worth.
tested_by: L13 question.how_money_works.013.q1; L13 question.how_money_works.013.q3; L14 question.how_money_works.014.q3; L20 question.how_money_works.020.q3

claim: The 50/30/20 rule is meant as a general guideline for dividing up a paycheck, not a precise law.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica Money: the 50-30-20 rule is not meant to be a budgetary precision law, but a general guideline. Acorns and other explainers call it a flexible starting point. (https://www.britannica.com/money/what-is-the-50-30-20-rule https://www.acorns.com/learn/saving/50-30-20-budget-rule/)

claim: Needs are expenses essential to survival and basic living, such as food, shelter, clothing and utilities; wants are things you desire for enjoyment or lifestyle.
fact_check_evidence: Experian: needs are expenses essential to survival (food, shelter, clothing, utilities and more); wants are for lifestyle or enjoyment. Britannica Money separates necessities (rent, utilities, groceries) from creature comforts in the same way. (https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/budgeting-needs-vs-wants/ https://www.britannica.com/money/what-is-the-50-30-20-rule)

claim: Within a need there can be a want: you need food, but dining out every night is a want.
fact_check_evidence: Experian: you need food, but dining out every night is a desire, not an essential expense. Britannica Money puts groceries under necessities and dining out under wants. (https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/budgeting-needs-vs-wants/ https://www.britannica.com/money/what-is-the-50-30-20-rule)

claim: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith defined necessaries as not only what is needed to support life, but whatever local custom makes it shameful for respectable people to be without.
fact_check_evidence: Wealth of Nations, Book V, Ch. 2: necessaries include not only what is indispensably necessary for life but whatever the custom of the country renders it indecent for creditable people to be without. Quoted identically by marxists.org and the Adam Smith Institute. (https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/smith-adam/works/wealth-of-nations/book05/ch02b-4.htm https://www.adamsmith.org/blog/on-the-subject-of-linen-shirts)

claim: Smith noted that a linen shirt is not strictly necessary for life, since the ancient Greeks and Romans lived comfortably without linen, yet a respectable day-labourer of his time would be ashamed to appear in public without one.
fact_check_evidence: Wealth of Nations, Book V, Ch. 2: a linen shirt is strictly speaking not a necessary of life; the Greeks and Romans lived comfortably without linen, but through most of Europe a creditable day-labourer would be ashamed to appear in public without one. (https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/smith-adam/works/wealth-of-nations/book05/ch02b-4.htm https://www.adamsmith.org/blog/on-the-subject-of-linen-shirts)

claim: Smith wrote that custom made leather shoes a necessity in England for men and women, in Scotland for men but not women, and in France for neither, where people could go in wooden shoes or barefoot without shame.
fact_check_evidence: Wealth of Nations, Book V, Ch. 2: leather shoes a necessary in England for both sexes; in Scotland for the lowest order of men but not women; in France for neither, who appear sometimes in wooden shoes and sometimes barefooted without discredit. (https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/smith-adam/works/wealth-of-nations/book05/ch02b-4.htm https://economistsview.typepad.com/economistsview/2006/03/adam_smith_on_r.html)

fact_check_evidence: The Decision Lab: adding a third, less attractive option (the decoy) can influence perception of the original two. Wikipedia (Decoy effect) gives the same definition. (https://thedecisionlab.com/biases/decoy-effect https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decoy_effect)

claim: A Visa or Mastercard payment involves four parties: the cardholder, the bank that issued the card, the merchant and the merchant's bank, called the acquirer.
fact_check_evidence: GAO-10-45: Visa and MasterCard transactions involve the issuing institution, the cardholder, the merchant and an acquiring institution. A Connecticut OLR report and Britannica Money describe the same parties. (https://www.gao.gov/assets/a298669.html https://www.cga.ct.gov/2013/rpt/2013-R-0015.htm)

claim: To authorize a card payment, the acquirer sends the request through the card network to the cardholder's issuing bank, which checks that the account is valid.
fact_check_evidence: GAO-10-45: acquirers forward the authorization request through the card network to the issuing institution, which authorizes it by verifying the account is valid. Payment-industry explainers (Stripe, Adyen) describe the same flow. (https://www.gao.gov/assets/a298669.html https://stripe.com/resources/more/interchange-fees-101-what-they-are-how-they-work-and-how-to-cut-costs)

claim: The acquirer then settles the purchase, paying the merchant's account with money from the issuer, minus the interchange fee and its own service fees.
fact_check_evidence: GAO-10-45: acquirers clear and settle card purchases by providing payment from the issuing institution to the merchant's account, except for the interchange fees and their own service fees. Britannica Money: the customer's bank collects the fee during settlement. (https://www.gao.gov/assets/a298669.html https://www.britannica.com/money/credit-card-interchange-fees)

claim: Merchants pay a merchant discount fee on card sales, and most of it goes from the acquirer to the card issuer as an interchange fee.
fact_check_evidence: GAO-10-45: the majority of the merchant discount fee is paid from the acquirer to the issuer as interchange, the largest portion of card acceptance fees. Britannica Money: merchants pay, and the customer's bank collects the fees. (https://www.gao.gov/assets/a298669.html https://www.britannica.com/money/credit-card-interchange-fees)

claim: Merchants pay a merchant discount fee on card sales, and most of it goes from the acquirer to the card issuer as an interchange fee.
fact_check_evidence: GAO-10-45: the majority of the merchant discount fee is paid from the acquirer to the issuer as interchange, the largest portion of card acceptance fees. Britannica Money: merchants pay, and the customer's bank collects the fees. (https://www.gao.gov/assets/a298669.html https://www.britannica.com/money/credit-card-interchange-fees)

fact_check_evidence: GAO-10-45: the card networks set the fees, which generally range from 1 to 3 percent of the purchase price. Britannica Money: the network creates the fee structure, typically 1.5% to 3% plus a small fixed fee. claim: A 2010 Boston Fed study found that because merchants generally charge card and cash users the same price, cash users in effect pay part of the cost of card fees and rewards.
fact_check_evidence: Boston Fed PPDP 10-3 abstract: merchant fees and rewards generate an implicit transfer to card users from cash users because merchants generally do not set different prices for card users. The paper is also hosted by the ECB and RePEc; a later PERC reexamination disputes the size of the transfer, not the mechanism. (https://www.bostonfed.org/publications/public-policy-discussion-paper/2010/who-gains-and-who-loses-from-credit-card-payments-theory-and-calibrations.aspx https://ideas.repec.org/p/fip/fedbpp/10-3.html https://www.perc.net/wp-content/uploads/2013/08/A-Reexamination-of-Who-Gains-and-Who-Loses-from-Credit-Card-Payments.pdf)

claim: In a 2022 C+R Research survey of 1,000 US consumers, people guessed they spent $86 a month on subscriptions; itemized, the average was $219.
fact_check_evidence: C+R Research: consumers first estimated $86 a month, but itemized spending averaged $219; 1,000 consumers surveyed April 22 to May 2, 2022. CNBC and NBC4 reported the same figures. (https://www.crresearch.com/blog/subscription-service-statistics-and-costs/ https://www.cnbc.com/2022/06/02/consumers-spend-133-more-monthly-on-subscriptions-than-they-realize.html)

claim: In the same survey, 74% said recurring subscription charges were easy to forget, and 42% had stopped using a subscription but forgot they were still paying for it.
fact_check_evidence: C+R Research: 74% said it was easy to forget recurring monthly subscription charges; 42% stopped using a service but forgot they were still paying. CNBC reported both figures. (https://www.crresearch.com/blog/subscription-service-statistics-and-costs/ https://www.cnbc.com/2022/06/02/consumers-spend-133-more-monthly-on-subscriptions-than-they-realize.html)

claim: The survey's gap of $133 a month between guessed and actual subscription spending adds up to $1,596 over 12 months.
fact_check_evidence: C+R Research: the gap between the $86 estimate and $219 actual is $133 a month (also reported by CNBC). $133 x 12 = $1,596 is exact arithmetic. (https://www.crresearch.com/blog/subscription-service-statistics-and-costs/ https://www.cnbc.com/2022/06/02/consumers-spend-133-more-monthly-on-subscriptions-than-they-realize.html)

claim: Spending $5 a day more on a bought lunch than a lunch from home adds up to $1,250 over 250 workdays, perhaps the cost of a decent vacation.
fact_check_evidence: OpenStax: $8 bought lunch vs $3 from home is a $5 daily opportunity cost; 250 days x $5 = $1,250, the cost perhaps of a decent vacation. The St. Louis Fed makes the same add-it-up point with a daily coffee. (https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/2-1-how-individuals-make-choices-based-on-their-budget-constraint https://www.stlouisfed.org/open-vault/2020/january/real-life-examples-opportunity-cost)

claim: Describing a small daily cost by what it adds up to, such as "a nice vacation" instead of "$5 a day", might lead you to make different choices.
fact_check_evidence: OpenStax: if you describe the opportunity cost as a nice vacation instead of $5 a day, you might make different choices. The St. Louis Fed urges the same reframing (what else the money could buy outright). (https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/2-1-how-individuals-make-choices-based-on-their-budget-constraint https://www.stlouisfed.org/open-vault/2020/january/real-life-examples-opportunity-cost)

claim: Prices falling in one sector because productivity is rising there are generally not a problem for the economy as a whole.
fact_check_evidence: Bernanke: sector-specific price declines from rising productivity 'are generally not a problem for the economy as a whole.' (https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/speeches/2002/20021121/default.htm https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deflation)

claim: Deflation is almost always a side effect of a collapse in spending so severe that producers must keep cutting prices to find buyers.
fact_check_evidence: Bernanke: deflation 'is in almost all cases a side effect of a collapse of aggregate demand', with producers cutting prices to find buyers. (https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/speeches/2002/20021121/default.htm https://www.federalreserveeducation.org/resources/lessons/lesson--great-depression-introduction-essay-wheelock.pdf)

claim: When prices are falling, people delay purchases if they can, which means less economic activity, less income and slower growth.
fact_check_evidence: IMF F&D: 'consumers delay making purchases if they can... less economic activity, less income generated by producers, and lower economic growth.' claim: When prices fall, borrowers must still repay the same amount of money, in dollars of ever-increasing real value.
fact_check_evidence: Bernanke: borrowers 'must still repay the principal in dollars of increasing (perhaps rapidly increasing) real value'. Wheelock: deflation 'increased the real burden of debt'. (https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/speeches/2002/20021121/default.htm https://www.federalreserveeducation.org/resources/lessons/lesson--great-depression-introduction-essay-wheelock.pdf)

claim: By 2002, a mild fall in Japanese consumer prices, about 1% a year, had come with years of painfully slow growth.

claim: In an arms race, two nations keep buying weapons; neither gains an advantage and both end up poorer.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: "When two nations keep buying more weapons... neither gains an advantage and both are poorer than when they started." (https://www.britannica.com/science/game-theory/The-prisoners-dilemma https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/prisoner-dilemma/)

claim: When the game repeats and players don't know which round is last, cooperation can emerge.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: with a fixed known number of rounds cooperation unravels, but "cooperation emerges when players don't know when the sequence ends." SEP discusses the same result for iterated play. (https://www.britannica.com/science/game-theory/The-prisoners-dilemma https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/prisoner-dilemma/)

claim: In Robert Axelrod's tournaments, Anatol Rapoport's tit for tat, cooperate first and then copy the partner's last move, did famously well.
fact_check_evidence: SEP: Rapoport's Tit for Tat succeeded in Axelrod's tournaments. Wikipedia and PLOS One describe it winning both of Axelrod's computer tournaments. (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/prisoner-dilemma/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tit_for_tat https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0134128)

claim: Axelrod found that every 'nice' strategy, one that never betrays first, beat every strategy that wasn't nice.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: Axelrod found that "every nice strategy outperformed every strategy that was not nice"; nice meaning never the first to defect. SEP discusses the same results. (https://www.britannica.com/science/game-theory/The-prisoners-dilemma https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/prisoner-dilemma/)

claim: Italian statistician Corrado Gini devised the Gini coefficient in 1912.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: developed by Italian statistician Corrado Gini in his 1912 paper Variabilita e mutabilita. Wikipedia agrees. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Gini-coefficient https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient)

claim: A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect equality; 1 means one person gets all the income and everyone else none.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: "A Gini of 0 indicates perfect equality, while 1 indicates that all income goes to one person and none to everyone else." The World Bank and Wikipedia use the same scale. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Gini-coefficient https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient)

claim: The Gini is tied to the Lorenz curve, a 1905 chart of what share of income goes to what share of people.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: closely tied to the Lorenz curve, developed in 1905 by Max Lorenz, which plots cumulative income share against cumulative population share. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Gini-coefficient https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient)

claim: The Gini shows how unequal a distribution is but not why; two countries with very different income patterns can share a score.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: the measure "shows how unequal a distribution is, but not why"; two countries with very different patterns can arrive at the same score. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Gini-coefficient https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient)

claim: Some countries measure consumption rather than income, which can miss how much wealth the richest households hold.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: in some nations the figure reflects consumption rather than income, failing to capture the extreme concentration of wealth among the richest households. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Gini-coefficient https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient)

claim: Wealth is a stock of resources you own; income is a flow of money coming in.
fact_check_evidence: OECD (2018) treats assets "as a stock of material resources complementary to a flow of current income." Economics texts draw the same stock-flow distinction. (https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2018/06/inequalities-in-household-wealth-across-oecd-countries_a91f464f/7e1bf673-en.pdf https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/society-at-a-glance-2024_918d8db3-en/full-report/income-and-wealth-inequalities_7ac4178f.html)

claim: Across 28 OECD countries, the richest 10% of households held 52% of household wealth; the top 10% of earners got 24% of income.
fact_check_evidence: OECD (2018): "the wealthiest 10% of households hold 52% of total net wealth, compared with 24% of total income held by the 10% of people at the top of the income distribution," across 28 countries. Society at a Glance 2024 reports a similar pattern. (https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2018/06/inequalities-in-household-wealth-across-oecd-countries_a91f464f/7e1bf673-en.pdf https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/society-at-a-glance-2024_918d8db3-en/full-report/income-and-wealth-inequalities_7ac4178f.html)

claim: On average, wealth inequality across OECD countries is about twice the level of income inequality.
fact_check_evidence: OECD (2018): "Wealth inequality is twice the level of income inequality on average." (https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2018/06/inequalities-in-household-wealth-across-oecd-countries_a91f464f/7e1bf673-en.pdf https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/society-at-a-glance-2024_918d8db3-en/full-report/income-and-wealth-inequalities_7ac4178f.html)

claim: An externality is the effect of a market exchange on a third party who is outside the exchange.
fact_check_evidence: OpenStax: "The effect of a market exchange on a third party who is outside or 'external' to the exchange is called an externality." Wikipedia defines it the same way. (https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/12-1-the-economics-of-pollution https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Externalities.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externality)

claim: An outdoor concert's noise affects neighbors who had no part in buying the tickets.
fact_check_evidence: OpenStax illustrates externalities with an outdoor arena whose concert noise affects nearby residents who had no role in the ticket purchase. (https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/12-1-the-economics-of-pollution)

claim: Pollution is a negative externality: a producer's costs cover labor and materials, but not the harm its pollution does to others.
fact_check_evidence: OpenStax: "Pollution is a negative externality"; it distinguishes private costs (labor, materials) from external pollution costs borne by society. Econlib calls air pollution a negative externality. (https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/12-1-the-economics-of-pollution https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Externalities.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externality)

claim: When firms don't pay for the pollution they cause, the market produces too much of the product.
fact_check_evidence: OpenStax: when firms ignore pollution costs, market equilibrium yields "too much of the product" compared with the socially optimal level. (https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/12-1-the-economics-of-pollution https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Externalities.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externality)

claim: Externalities can be positive too; research and development is a standard example.
fact_check_evidence: Econlib: "Research and development is a standard example of a positive externality." Wikipedia lists R&D and education among positive externalities. (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Externalities.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externality)

claim: Economist Arthur Pigou's most influential work was The Economics of Welfare, published in 1920.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: "Pigou's most influential work was The Economics of Welfare (1920)." The PMC centenary tribute agrees. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Arthur-Cecil-Pigou https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7814863/)

claim: Pigou argued that negative externalities should be offset by a tax and positive externalities by a subsidy.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: Pigou argued negative externalities "should be offset by a tax, while positive externalities should be offset by a subsidy." Wikipedia on Pigouvian taxes agrees. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Arthur-Cecil-Pigou https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigouvian_tax)

claim: A carbon tax is a modern Pigouvian tax, ideally set equal to the social cost of carbon.
fact_check_evidence: PMC tribute: "A Pigouvian tax on carbon emissions has to be set equal to the social cost of carbon." Wikipedia cites carbon taxes as a Pigouvian example. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7814863/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigouvian_tax)

claim: Ronald Coase challenged Pigou's approach in his 1960 paper 'The Problem of Social Cost'.
fact_check_evidence: Econlib: before Coase, economists accepted Pigou's view; Coase's 1960 "The Problem of Social Cost" challenged it. Wikipedia on the Coase theorem agrees. (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/Coase.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem)

claim: Coase's example: a rancher whose cattle damage a neighbor's crops, and a farmer who could pay the rancher to keep fewer cattle.
fact_check_evidence: Econlib: a steer earns the rancher $2 but causes $3 of crop damage, so the farmer would pay up to $3 for the rancher to reduce his herd. (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/Coase.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem)

claim: Coase showed that if deals cost little to make, the parties can bargain to an efficient outcome without government, whoever the law favors.
fact_check_evidence: Econlib Externalities: "as long as transactions costs are low, then the affected parties negotiate tolerably efficient solutions without government intervention"; efficiency doesn't depend on which party the law favors. (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/Coase.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Externalities.html)

claim: Coase showed that if deals cost little to make, the parties can bargain to an efficient outcome without government, whoever the law favors.
fact_check_evidence: Econlib Externalities: "as long as transactions costs are low, then the affected parties negotiate tolerably efficient solutions without government intervention"; efficiency doesn't depend on which party the law favors. (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/Coase.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Externalities.html)

claim: The costs of making a deal vary from negligible to enormous.
fact_check_evidence: Econlib Externalities: "every exchange has some transactions costs, which vary from negligible ... to enormous." Wikipedia on the Coase theorem stresses the same limit. (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/Externalities.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem)

claim: Coase won the 1991 economics Nobel for his work on transaction costs and property rights.
fact_check_evidence: Econlib: Nobel "for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights." Britannica lists the 1991 prize. (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/Coase.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem)

claim: In 1930, Keynes predicted living standards four to eight times higher a century later, and a 15-hour work week.
fact_check_evidence: The essay says the standard of life "a hundred years hence will be between 4 and 8 times as high" and mentions "a fifteen-hour week"; Crafts (2022) and Quote Investigator summarize the same prediction. (https://www.marxists.org/reference/subject/economics/keynes/1930/our-grandchildren.htm https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/research/workingpapers/2021/twerp_1360_-_crafts.pdf https://quoteinvestigator.com/2025/02/03/work-week/)

claim: In 1930, Keynes predicted living standards four to eight times higher a century later, and a 15-hour work week.
fact_check_evidence: The essay says the standard of life "a hundred years hence will be between 4 and 8 times as high" and mentions "a fifteen-hour week"; Crafts (2022) and Quote Investigator summarize the same prediction. (https://www.marxists.org/reference/subject/economics/keynes/1930/our-grandchildren.htm https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/research/workingpapers/2021/twerp_1360_-_crafts.pdf https://quoteinvestigator.com/2025/02/03/work-week/)

claim: Economist Nicholas Crafts concluded that Keynes's 15-hour week will not arrive by 2030.
fact_check_evidence: Crafts abstract: "In 1930 Keynes opined that by 2030 people would work only 15 hours per week. As such, this prediction will not be realised." A BLS summary also notes no shift to a 15-hour week. (https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/research/workingpapers/2021/twerp_1360_-_crafts.pdf https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ecca.12439)

claim: UK expected lifetime hours of leisure and home production rose 58% from 1931 to 2011, reflecting longer lives and longer retirements.
fact_check_evidence: Crafts abstract: expected lifetime hours of leisure and home production in the UK "rose by 58 per cent between 1931 and 2011", reflecting life expectancy at older ages and longer retirements. (https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/research/workingpapers/2021/twerp_1360_-_crafts.pdf https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ecca.12439)

claim: Behavioral economists find that simple details, like the default option (what happens unless you choose otherwise), shape decisions.
fact_check_evidence: Nobel 2017: improvements "often involve simple things, such as how the default option is defined - the one that is the result unless you actively choose something else." Madrian and Shea (2001) found automatic enrollment sharply raised 401(k) participation. (https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/popular-economicsciences2017-1.pdf https://www.nber.org/papers/w7682)

claim: Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow plan uses the fact that promising to save more in the future, especially after a raise, feels easier.
fact_check_evidence: Nobel 2017: "It is often easier to promise to save more in the future, particularly if they expect their salary to increase. This insight has been used in the Save More Tomorrow programme" by Thaler and Benartzi. (https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/popular-economicsciences2017-1.pdf https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2017/press-release/)

claim: Some critics call such programs paternalistic; supporters stress that joining is voluntary and people can opt out at any time.
fact_check_evidence: Nobel 2017: "this type of programme has been criticised for being paternalistic, but ... joining the programme is completely voluntary and ... participants are free to opt out from it at any time." (https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/popular-economicsciences2017-1.pdf https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2017/press-release/)

claim: The sunk cost effect is a greater tendency to keep going with something once money, effort or time has been invested in it.
fact_check_evidence: Arkes and Blumer (1985) abstract: "The sunk cost effect is manifested in a greater tendency to continue an endeavor once an investment in money, effort, or time has been made." Quoted widely, e.g. ResearchGate copy. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0749597885900494 https://www.coglode.com/research/sunk-cost-effect https://www.researchgate.net/publication/4812596_The_psychology_of_sunk_cost)

claim: In a 1985 study, theater-goers randomly charged full price for season tickets went to more plays over the next six months than those given discounts.
fact_check_evidence: Arkes and Blumer (1985): customers who paid more for a season subscription attended more plays during the next six months; Coglode: full-price buyers used more tickets than those at either discount. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0749597885900494 https://www.coglode.com/research/sunk-cost-effect https://www.researchgate.net/publication/4812596_The_psychology_of_sunk_cost)
